messages.subject: Two-dim "Mixture-model" with Log-normal distributed data and normal uncertainty
parts:
Dear stan community,

I have the following question and I am thankful for any help. As I am a total noob with statistical inference, I hope that this question is not too trivial.

I have a dataset, which is theoretically described by a Log-Normall distribution. The measuring process adds systematically an unknown constant to this distribution and a normal distributed noise.
My model looks like:

data {
  int<lower=0> NumData;
  real InData[NumData];
}

parameters {
  real                   LN_mean; 
  real<lower=0>  LN_sigma; 
  real                   mean_FB;
  real<lower=0>  scatter;
  real<lower=0>  mydata_true[NumData];
}

model {
  LN_mean  ~ uniform(-6, +6);
  LN_sigma ~ uniform( 0, +6);
  mean_FB  ~ uniform(-6, +6);
  scatter       ~ uniform( 0, +6);

  for (i in 1:NumData)
  {
    mydata_true[i] ~ lognormal(LN_mean, LN_sigma);
    InData[i]      ~ normal(mean_FB + mydata_true[i], scatter);
  }
}

I get the error message "The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected... Scale parameter is inf, but must be finite!", which I hope is fine, as it is sporadically (~20 times, depending on the number of input data).
I want now to extend this model, as in reality the data are drawn from few log-normal distributions with different means and std.dev's.
My model looks like (Manual page 104): 

data {
  int<lower=1>  NumData;
  int<lower=1>  NumMixtures;
  real                 InData[NumData];
}

parameters {
  simplex[NumMixtures] Mixing_proportions;
  real                              My_means [NumMixtures]; 
  real<lower=0>             My_sigmas[NumMixtures]; 
}

model {

  real ps[NumMixtures];  
  My_means  ~ normal(0,5);
  My_sigmas ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

  for (n in 1:NumData)
  {
     for (k in 1:NumMixtures)
     {
        ps[k] <- log(Mixing_proportions[k]) + normal_log(True_Data[n], My_means[k], My_sigmas[k]);
     }
     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
  }
}

But I have no idea how to include now the normal noise with mean and scatter. I also cannot write the first(1-Dim) example as sum of log-likelihood, as this is the convolution of the normal with the log-normal. Do I have to include an numerical integration for this? Is there a smart/efficient way around?

Any help/suggestions are appreciated.
Thanks,
Lukas

Your model's not identified, so there are going to be problems.

Usually a noisy measurement model is assuming that the "true" value
of something being measured is equal to the measurement plus some
noise (often just centered normal).

> I get the error message "The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected... Scale parameter is inf, but must be finite!", which I hope is fine, as it is sporadically (~20 times, depending on the number of input data).

Your parameters need to be declared with lower
and upper bound that matches the constraints in the model.
So this is incompatible:

> real LN_mean;
> LN_mean ~ uniform(-6, +6);

Constraint entails (-inf, inf) are valid whereas support is
only on (-6, 6). You need to fix this for *all* of your
parameters.

We don't recommend using these priors, by the way. See the
regression chapter of the manual for discussion.

Then when that's fixed, try simulating data from the model
then fitting it.

I don't quite understand here what you're trying to do, because
I didn't understand the intention of your first noisy measurement

Whatever you do, you probably want to provide a hierarchical

I was thinking about the mathematical expression for the likelihood. In the one-temperatrure model it is a convolution of the real underlying distribution (log-normal) with the noise (normal)  i.e. the probability of observing x_obs is :
 
(1)   p (x_obs) = INTEGRAL dx p_lognormal (x ,LN_mu, LN_sigma) * p_normal (x_obs - x, FB_mu, scatter)

integrated over the support of X. For the two temperature model it should be:

p(x_obs) = proportion p_1(x_obs) + (1-proportion) p_2(x_obs)

where p_1/2 are the probabilities defined in (1) but with different parameters for LN_mu_1/2 and LN_sigma_1/2.

The (weak) identification problem is in FB_mu + mydata_true[i].
You can subtract a number from FB_mu and add it to all the mydata_true and
get the same likelihood. This is very typical in hierarchical models (which
have same structure as your model).

Your model also has LN_mu to take up the slack for FB_mu. So the only thing
identifiying this is the priors. But the Cauchy is a weak, fat-tailed prior by
construction so it can give you problems in practice when you try to use it to
control the location of a bunch of parameters.

If you can fit simulated data to it, then it may not be a big
deal in practice. There's a discussion of identifiability issues and
what they do to sampling in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

- Bob

This is really just a latent variable model — i.e. don’t
think about mydata_true as data but rather as some
latent state describing the underlying source of the radiation.

From this perspective the mixture is no problem — you
just write the latent luminosity as coming from a mixture
of the high and low sources,

for (n in 1:n_data) {
latent_luminosity[n] ~ increment_log_prob(
log_mix(theta,
lognormal_log(low_mu, low_sigma),
lognormal_log(high_mu, high_sigma)));
measured_luminosity[n] ~ normal(latent_luminosity[n] + offset, scatter);
}

Here theta is the creative proportion of the two components
in your medium. If you really want to go crazy you could
make theta depend on other parameters, but you should
start simple.

Also be careful with that assumed normal on the data. It
should probably be a log_normal given the positivity
constraint (here you’re hoping that the measurements
are large enough that the normal is an okay approximation).

This is really just a latent variable model — i.e. don’t
think about mydata_true as data but rather as some
latent state describing the underlying source of the radiation.

From this perspective the mixture is no problem — you
just write the latent luminosity as coming from a mixture
of the high and low sources,

for (n in 1:n_data) {
  latent_luminosity[n] ~ increment_log_prob(
                                       log_mix(theta,
                                                     lognormal_log(low_mu, low_sigma),
                                                     lognormal_log(high_mu, high_sigma)));
  measured_luminosity[n] ~ normal(latent_luminosity[n] + offset, scatter);
}

Here theta is the creative proportion of the two components
in your medium.  If you really want to go crazy you could
make theta depend on other parameters, but you should
start simple.

Also be careful with that assumed normal on the data.  It
should probably be a log_normal given the positivity
constraint (here you’re hoping that the measurements
are large enough that the normal is an okay approximation).

Hi Lukas,

When you say that it doesn't work out anymore, I'm assuming you mean that it doesn't produce the same results. If it's not running any more, then let us know -- that's something different.

If it's what I suspect (different results), it's because the model is different. Let's look at the log_mix part of the model:
for (i in 1 : num_data) {
    increment_log_prob(log_mix(Proportion,
lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_low , sigma_low ),

lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_high, sigma_high)));
}

vs.

increment_log_prob(log_mix(Proportion,

lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_low , sigma_low ),
                                               lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_high, sigma_high)));

In the first section, the Proportion parameter is the mixture between individual components -- on the probability scale:
(Proportion * lognormal(Latent_Data[1], mu_low, sigma_low) + (1 - Proportion) * lognormal(Latent_Data[1], mu_high, sigma_high)) * (Proportion * lognormal(Latent_Data[2], mu_low, sigma_low) + (1 - Proportion) * lognormal(Latent_Data[2], mu_high, sigma_high)) + ...

In the second, the Proportion parameter is the mixture between two models. On the probability scale:
Proportion * lognormal(Latent_Data, mu_low, sigma_low) + (1 - Proportion) * lognormal(Latent_Data, mu_high, sigma_high)

where lognormal(Latent_Data, mu, sigma) = \sum_{i = 1}^num_data lognormal(Latent_Data[i], mu, sigma)


These are just different models. Let me know if that wasn't clear and I'll try again, or you can try to work out the math.

> On Mon, Aug 10, 2015 at 4:46 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just to make sure I understand you Daniel, the first version is demanding that every datum is a blend of the two models with the set proportion,
>
> yes.
>
> whereas the second is treating the data as a whole as a blend of two models with said proportion,
>
> yes.
>
> but any one datum's contribution can be of a different "proportonal mix" as it were?
>
> umm. I think it can be viewed as each datum's contribution is equal. I think?

Since this is confusing a lot of people, I'll add a compare-and-contrast
section to the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1526#issuecomment-129711045

A mixture model assumes each observation comes from one of the mixture
components. In the binary mixture of normal case, that's

z[n] ~ bernoulli(lambda);
y[n] ~ normal(mu[z[n] + 1], sigma[z[n] + 1]);

But when you marginalize out the discrete "responsibility"
parameter z, you get something that looks like what you call
a "proportional mix",

p(y[n]|lambda, mu, sigma) = lambda * normal(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2])
+ (1 - lambda) * normal(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1])

- Bob

> Since this is confusing a lot of people, I'll add a compare-and-contrast
> section to the manual:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1526#issuecomment-129711045
>
> A mixture model assumes each observation comes from one of the mixture
> components. In the binary mixture of normal case, that's
>
> z[n] ~ bernoulli(lambda);
> y[n] ~ normal(mu[z[n] + 1], sigma[z[n] + 1]);
>
> But when you marginalize out the discrete "responsibility"
> parameter z, you get something that looks like what you call
> a "proportional mix",
>
> p(y[n]|lambda, mu, sigma) = lambda * normal(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2])
> + (1 - lambda) * normal(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1])
>
